findings.description: storage_encrypted = false leaves the RDS MySQL instance storage, snapshots, and logs unencrypted, so any access to the underlying volume or a shared snapshot exposes database contents in cleartext.

publicly_accessible = true gives the database a public endpoint reachable from the internet (and the endpoint is exported as a Terraform output), removing the network boundary that should isolate the data tier and combining badly with the default 'admin' user and unencrypted storage.

The master username is the predictable default 'admin' and the password comes from a plain Terraform variable that is stored in cleartext in state and interpolated into EC2 user data, instead of using Secrets Manager / managed master password or IAM database authentication.

The user_data script writes the RDS master username and var.password in cleartext into /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc; user data is readable from the instance metadata service by any local process or via SSRF, and is visible in the EC2 console and Terraform state, leaking database master credentials.

No metadata_options block enforcing http_tokens = "required", so IMDSv1 remains enabled. Combined with a PHP application that processes user input and a highly privileged instance profile, an SSRF can harvest the ec2role credentials and the plaintext database password from user data.
No root_block_device encryption is configured, so the instance volume that stores the plaintext dbinfo.inc credentials file may be written to an unencrypted EBS volume and snapshots.

The inline policy grants s3:*, ec2:*, and rds:* on Resource "*". Because this role is attached via the instance profile to an internet-facing web server, compromise of that instance yields full control over all S3 data, EC2 infrastructure, and RDS databases in the account, including privilege escalation paths.

The RDS security group allows MySQL (3306) ingress from the entire VPC CIDR rather than only from the application instance's security group, so any workload anywhere in the VPC can reach the database directly.
The database security group permits all protocols and ports outbound to 0.0.0.0/0, providing an unrestricted channel for data exfiltration or command-and-control from a compromised database tier.

The MySQL parameter group sets only character-set parameters and does not set require_secure_transport = 1, so the publicly accessible database accepts unencrypted client connections (the PHP app connects with mysqli_connect without TLS), allowing credentials and data to be intercepted.
